title: The Succession That Was Not
text:
Nineteen winters ago the Azure Cloud had three candidates for the Sword-Peak Hall, and a fourth whose name was not written anywhere: a middling disciple named Jin Wuan, the elder uncle of a boy now wearing no sash. Jin Wuan favoured a harsher reading of the sect's charter — harsh enough that the three named candidates withdrew rather than stand against him, and the Elder Council sat in silence for seven days. On the eighth Jin Wuan left of his own accord, 'to walk the grey,' his written note said. He was never seen on Azure ground again.

Elder Baixu will tell you, if asked at the right moment, that the charter was wrong and Jin Wuan was right, and the price of being right was paid by the nephew. He will not tell you what his own role in those seven days was. He will let the silence sit between the two of you, and then refill your cup.

title: Mingshu's Last Silence
text:
When the Heart-Devouring Gale Tiger fell at last, its four open eyes closed in order, like shutters on four rooms going dark. The Patriarch, who had knelt four hundred years beside his youngest, did not stand. He turned his face to the wind, lifted one hand — the hand that had cut the boy's first sword-scar into the air ten thousand times, finishing what the child had never lived to finish — and bowed. The scar completed itself in the stone. The ghost thinned. The wind took him, quieter this time, the way a long breath leaves a long body.

Only you heard the last word. It was not 'don't,' as legend has recorded it. It was the youngest disciple's name.

title: Four Reasons the Pavilion Refuses
text:
Elder Red Feather, when she trusts you with it, will name the four reasons the Scarlet Lotus Pavilion will refuse a contract — any contract, at any price, for any buyer:

  One: against a child, whose debts are not yet theirs.
  Two: against a cook or physician, whose hands feed and mend and ask no name.
  Three: against the last of a line, for then grief has no one to give itself to.
  Four: for the joy of it, which is a thing we do not sell.

'Everything else,' she says, 'is a question of the price. We name the price aloud — the buyer, the seller, the dead. This is our kindness. It is the only kindness we have.'

title: The Five Refusals
text:
At the taking of the first poison, a Five Poisons initiate speaks the five refusals into a cup of black-water, and drinks. The initiate says:

  'I refuse to lie about the bite. I refuse to hide the fang.
   I refuse the righteous mouth that pretends the price is not paid.
   I refuse the demonic hand that pretends the price is the reward.
   I refuse the merchant who would sell the antidote to the victim and the poison to the feast.'

Matriarch Shan will pass you the cup, if you have earned it. The black-water is sweet. Most who drink it weep, though nobody asks about what.

title: The Eight-Point Star's Ledger
text:
The Stormcaller disciple's brand — the eight-pointed star of the Heavenly Sword Tower — is not only safe-conduct and debt. Each point is a kill that the Tower has accepted as payment toward graduation. Recruits begin with zero; most never reach eight; the few who do are turned out of the Tower on the same day, because a graduate cannot be a disciple.

The one you have killed was at six. He will not graduate. The Tower will record his death as partial payment against his uncle's debt — the uncle you have not yet met, who collects on Sky-Spire in a cloak the colour of old iron.

title: The Dancers on the Hanging Terraces
text:
Before the Jadestep Sect claimed the cliffs, the Hanging Terraces were said to be a dancing-floor for the wind-spirits who feared the earth. A dancer stepped so lightly on the jade lattices that the lattices sang and did not crack, and the lowland farmers looked up at night to see the cliffs glowing like lanterns as the sky-women turned.

The Jadestep founders are said to have bargained with the dancers for the use of the terraces. In exchange, the cliffs would always hold one sword-saint, living or remembering. When the last of them falls, the dancers come back for the terraces — and for whoever has been foolish enough to stand on them.
